I was in a dilemma lately. I had all these opinions and thoughts about almost any topic, but the problem was, I didn't know who I wanted to share them with. Who am I kidding — the real reason I didn't want to share was because of the consequences. I'm still building myself up: to be better, to have a better job, to be more stable, to earn a higher pay. All those things I want, my dreams, might not happen because of my opinions, because of a post that the public might not agree with or might flame me for. I was afraid. Afraid that the things I say could impact how I'm perceived. That anxious feeling is the main reason I don't feel like sharing anything.

Yet, so many of the best, most powerful, and influential people got to where they are by sharing their opinions. Words can be incredibly powerful and impactful. Listening to smart, charismatic people on podcasts has really opened my eyes to that. It's motivated me to find my own voice, to have the courage to write and share my thoughts.

So in the past few weeks, after finally learning how to set up Hermes, learning to use Linux, and having my own agent, I feel like I am ready to make my voice and my writing public. I set up a blog. Yeah, yeah, anticlimactic I know. But it does feel good seeing it run live, especially since it was made by Hermes. I had it set up now... what should I talk about? That's the beautiful part — I can literally write about anything. *"Cows actually can fly."* *"Blackholes are just propaganda from NASA to get funds."* *"Moon Landing was not real."* *"The Earth is actually flat."* Okay, okay, I'm just playing around. I guess I'll just write about what I listened to on podcasts this week.

---

### The Power of Storytelling & Documentation

One podcast that really resonated with me was from Shahril Hamdan's show *Keris & Silicon*. He had a fascinating dialogue with Gita Wirjawan, an Indonesian businessman, former Trade Minister, and founder of an investment firm. Wirjawan offered an interesting perspective on why our Southeast Asian history has often been based more on assumptions than concrete evidence. As he explained simply: 

> *"We were never good at storytelling."*

Our ancestors simply didn't have the habit of documenting and recording things the way other cultures did. It's a shame, because written history can be so powerful in shaping a nation's narrative.

Wirjawan's insights made me reflect on how the lack of historical documentation has impacted our collective understanding of Malaysia's past. Without robust records and firsthand accounts, we're left to fill in the gaps through speculation and interpretation. This lack of a strong storytelling tradition is something Wirjawan believes has hindered our ability to definitively capture and share our national heritage. Hearing his perspective on this really struck a chord with me and gave me a newfound appreciation for the importance of writing and preserving one's history.

---

### Reflections on Merdeka

Now, as I'm writing this, it's almost Malaysia's Independence Day, and I have reflected a lot on our nation. As a devout Muslim, I have always wondered what I did to deserve to be born here. Malaysia is perfect. I'm not saying that just because I'm proud, although I am — but hear me out:

- **Geographically:** We are in the best spot, not directly above the Ring of Fire, serving as a natural bridge between the West and the East, with one of the oldest rainforests in the world.
- **Time & Rhythm:** Time-wise, it's so perfect for a Muslim, from sunrise to sunset.
- **Economically:** We have rich natural resources, a quality workforce, leading semiconductor industries, vibrant tourism, multicultural harmony, beaches, lakes, mountains, waterfalls, and iconic skyscrapers.
- **Values:** But the most important part for me is the values. We have embedded Islamic values so deeply into our country. We are pioneers in integrating Islamic principles into everything — food, economics, and even the little everyday conveniences like bidets, which are easily accessible everywhere.

Look, everything has a flaw, but come on. I am grateful to the Almighty to be born here, and to call myself a proud Malaysian. 

**Happy Independence Day!**
